extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policymakers, and industry practitioners working on data center operations, sustainability reporting, and environmental/health impact assessment (e.g., data center operators, AI infrastructure teams, environmental modelers, public health economists)
extracted.subtask_description: Quantify and mitigate the public-health impacts of data centers by modeling lifecycle pollutant emissions, estimating associated health costs, and integrating health metrics into geo‑distributed load balancing and operational decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary evaluation metrics for GLB algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare geo‑distributed load balancing (GLB) approaches on health cost, electricity (energy) cost, and carbon emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports health cost (Million $), energy cost (Million $), and carbon (Million Ton) and uses percent changes vs baseline to show tradeoffs (e.g., HI‑GLB achieved ~26% reduction in health cost, 3% electricity cost saving, and >1% carbon reduction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of marginal carbon emission rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Use marginal carbon emissions rates (rather than average carbon intensity) to quantify carbon impacts when comparing to marginal health prices and evaluating demand‑side load shifting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification: marginal metrics better reflect actual system‑wide carbon impacts resulting from demand‑side actions. The paper uses WattTime marginal carbon emission rates for fair comparison with marginal health price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of WattTime health price and industry electricity prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use WattTime's health price signal for each data center location and industry electricity prices from the EIA when estimating location‑specific health and electricity costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied per‑location 2023 values (WattTime health price; EIA industrial electricity price). These signals are the inputs to HI‑GLB and comparisons with carbon‑aware GLB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carbon‑price sensitivity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating carbon‑aware GLB, vary the carbon price pc over a policy‑relevant range to assess sensitivity of health and cost outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study varies pc from $5/ton to $200/ton (consistent with prior U.S. administrations) and includes special cases $0/ton (pure electricity cost optimization) and $∞/ton (pure carbon minimization) to illustrate extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt health‑informed computing as an explicit optimization metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate public health risk (health price / health cost) explicitly as a key metric when scheduling data center workloads or designing GLB algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HI‑GLB integrates a health price into the cost function to directly reduce health burden; comparison shows that carbon optimization alone may increase health costs while HI‑GLB reduces health costs substantially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use COBRA Desktop v5.1 for public health impact estimation (county level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the U.S. EPA COBRA (Desktop v5.1, Oct 2024) reduced‑complexity screening model to estimate county‑level public health impacts from emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COBRA uses a source–receptor matrix for rapid evaluation; its accuracy has been validated and it is commonly adopted for large‑area air quality and health impact analysis. Limit analysis to the geographic coverage supported by COBRA (contiguous U.S., county units).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary and discounting assumptions for health valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Present monetary values in constant 2023 U.S. dollars and set the discount rate to 2% (per OMB Circular No. A‑4) when using COBRA valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting a single value or ratio, use the midrange of COBRA's low and high estimates. Note that projections and inflation adjustments can change health‑to‑electricity cost ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data handling for multi‑year estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Use COBRA's provided county‑level data for 2016, 2023, and 2028; for intermediate years (2019–2022) apply linear interpolation as recommended by the COBRA team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cities considered county‑equivalents in COBRA should be treated as 'counties' in the analysis. Use midrange when reporting single-point estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope definitions and reporting protocol recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardize reporting of criteria air pollutants by categorizing into three scopes (analogous to GHG scopes) and report public‑health impacts following the Greenhouse Gas Protocol conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation rationale: criteria air pollutants are overlooked in AI model cards and sustainability reports; adopting scope‑1/2/3 reporting for pollutants enables transparent, demand‑side solutions and cross‑company comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average attribution method for scope‑2 (electricity) impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: For scope‑2 (electricity‑attributed) impacts, use the average attribution method: compute the fraction x% = e_DC / e_total for each electricity region and scale region baseline emissions by x% in COBRA to estimate data center attributable impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation details: divide the U.S. grid into 14 regions per AVERT v4.3, use state‑level data center electricity distribution from EPRI scaled to total consumption, and apportion state consumption to AVERT regions. The relationship between health impact and emission reduction in COBRA is approximately linear, enabling proportional scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling missing scope‑1 emissions data
rubrics_metrics.description: When scope‑1 (on‑site) emission data are unavailable, estimate using emission rates derived from a reference jurisdiction (Virginia) multiplied by the state's data center energy consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: this introduces estimation error but is acceptable because scope‑2 health costs are substantially more dominant in total impacts. Make assumptions explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption for backup generator actual emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: When using permit limits to estimate backup generator impacts, assume actual emissions are a fraction of permitted levels (the paper assumes 10% of permitted levels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Virginia permitted totals → assume 10% actual emissions to estimate asthma cases, deaths, and annual public health burden ($220–300 million total annually). Document source of permits and time window (permits before Jan 1, 2023 and between Jan 1, 2023–Dec 1, 2024 were combined here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial correlation and variability analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze spatial relationships between health prices and carbon emission rates using correlation coefficients (e.g., Pearson) and visualizations (CDFs, scatter plots) to identify conflicts or co‑benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreting results: e.g., a Pearson correlation ≈ -0.35 indicates a negative relationship suggesting potential conflict between carbon optimization and health outcomes; also examine spatial variability (health prices may vary more across regions than carbon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authoritative, transparent data sources and mapping procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on established public data sources (WattTime for signals, EIA for electricity prices and plant data, EPRI for data center electricity distribution, AVERT for region mapping, COBRA for health impacts) and document apportionment/mapping procedures (state→region, power plant attribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: state‑level industrial electricity prices from EIA, marginal carbon and health signals from WattTime, AVERT region apportionment, and EPRI state distributions scaled to national totals. Document versions (e.g., COBRA Desktop v5.1, AVERT v4.3) and any scaling or interpolation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity and cross‑state impact consideration in siting and procurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate and disclose cross‑state distributional public health burdens (including affected communities far from data center sites) and prioritize interventions to address disproportionate impacts on disadvantaged communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations include holistically evaluating cross‑state burdens when siting data centers, sourcing electricity, and installing renewables; prioritize interdisciplinary research (cross‑state dispersion, health economics) and ensure reporting shows distributional metrics (e.g., per‑household health cost ratios across counties).
